This study examines the two-point functions within the perturbative framework of gravity theories featuring a cosmological constant, specifically focusing on the interaction between topology-changing and non-changing processes. We demonstrate that this interplay yields a distinctive behavior in the two-point functions, which we attribute to the presence of a non-trivial nonlocal component.

This study examines the link between Twitter account suspensions and rule violations. We analyzed a dataset comprising 100,000 suspended accounts and 100,000 randomly selected active accounts, comparing their rule-breaking rates. Our findings indicate that suspended users commit violations at a rate 1.5 times higher than their active counterparts. Additionally, we investigated the relationship between suspensions and the volume of rule-breaking tweets, discovering that suspended users generate fewer such tweets on average compared to active users.

The LHCb detector, designed for electron-hadron collisions, is being upgraded to function as a hadron collider experiment. This transformation will enable the facility to support hadron-hadron collision studies, thereby expanding its scientific reach. This paper outlines the upgrade's technical specifications and examines how the resulting capabilities will influence future experimental designs.

This study introduces a novel ensemble modeling approach designed to enhance the accuracy of neural network classification in scenarios involving noisy labels. The method leverages the inherent diversity of neural networks to construct an ensemble of models, each trained on a distinct subset of the data. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that this strategy significantly mitigates the impact of label noise. Empirical results across various benchmark datasets confirm that the proposed approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

This paper introduces a novel resource allocation framework for V2X communications, designed to optimize the transmission of safety messages. The approach employs a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) algorithm to train a neural network that assigns resources to vehicles based on their specific needs. The system's reward function is defined by the packet delivery ratio (PDR) of safety messages, while the action space encompasses all available V2X resources. The network is trained using a simulation environment that models V2X interactions and evaluates the resulting PDR. The study demonstrates that this method outperforms existing schemes, particularly in high-crash-risk scenarios, by prioritizing vehicles with elevated accident probabilities.

The rapid advancement of AI has sparked significant public concern regarding fairness and transparency. Consequently, there is a growing demand for explainable AI (XAI) to clarify the reasoning behind AI decisions. This paper introduces a novel framework for explaining AI-generated images, utilizing a multi-modal approach that integrates both visual and textual data. We propose a new metric to evaluate the quality of these explanations, and we conduct a comprehensive analysis of various existing metrics. Furthermore, we present a new method for generating explanations that leverages the capabilities of large language models.

Feature toggles are a software development technique that allows teams to merge code into a main branch without immediately deploying it to users. This study investigates the impact of using feature toggles on the frequency of branch merges and the duration of the development lifecycle. By analyzing 1,000 commits across 100 projects, we found that projects utilizing feature toggles experience branch merges 1.5 times more often and achieve a development lifecycle that is 1.5 times shorter compared to those that do not.

This study examines the link between conservation laws and symmetries within the context of the two-dimensional incompressible Euler equations. We demonstrate that the conservation of total enstropy arises from an accidental symmetry, a concept also applicable to the conservation of total energy in the Hamiltonian framework. Furthermore, we show that the conservation of total kinetic energy corresponds to a gauge symmetry, a finding that extends to the Hamiltonian description of the two-dimensional Euler equations.

This paper introduces Maximum Attention, a novel visualization technique designed to enhance the interpretability of trained neural networks. By leveraging the maximum value of the attention map across all channels, Maximum Attention highlights the specific regions of interest within an input image that the network prioritizes. This approach offers a more comprehensive view of the features the network concentrates on, surpassing the limitations of traditional attention maps that display only a single channel. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Maximum Attention can be seamlessly integrated into existing attention mechanisms, such as the CBAM, to improve their interpretability. Experimental results indicate that this method not only enhances interpretability but also boosts the performance of the CBAM model.

This study examines loop-level corrections to the scattering of two massive spin-2 particles into two massless spin-2 particles, mediated by new massive spin-2 fields. We demonstrate that these loop effects significantly alter the results of the corresponding tree-level calculations.

This paper introduces a new framework for analyzing war and peace negotiations, one that explicitly accounts for political bias. We demonstrate that bias influences the anticipated outcomes for a state, even when the state's actual preferences remain constant. Furthermore, we show that bias can lead to the escalation of conflicts despite the absence of a rational basis for doing so.

This study investigates the neural mechanisms underlying sentence processing, specifically how the brain links fillers to their corresponding thematic roles. We employed a multivariate analysis of EEG data collected from participants reading sentences containing both valid and invalid fillers. The findings revealed that neural patterns associated with the assignment of fillers to roles overlapped across different sentence types, indicating that the brain processes these thematic bindings in a distributed manner. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that the brain's neural architecture is capable of encoding the complex syntactic and semantic relationships inherent in natural language.

This study examines the potential for neutrino observatories to localize transient events originating from gravitational wave interferometers. We demonstrate that the angular precision of neutrino candidates is sufficient to significantly narrow down the search area for triggers detected by gravitational wave detectors. Furthermore, we show that the timing accuracy of neutrino events can further refine the localization of gravitational wave triggers.

This study investigates the impact of mirror seeing on the spatial power spectrum density (PSD) of wavefront errors in the context of the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). We demonstrate that the spatial PSD amplitude is directly proportional to the primary mirror's condition, whereas its spatial frequency distribution remains unaffected by mirror seeing. Consequently, the spatial PSD serves as a reliable metric for assessing the state of the primary mirror.

The recently developed r2SCAN density functional has been integrated with the PHONOPY code to facilitate phonon dispersion calculations for materials modeled using r2SCAN. This study demonstrates the method's application by calculating phonon dispersions for silicon and diamond.

This framework demonstrates that coverability sets for Very-WSTS can be computed as fixed points of monotone, continuous coverability relations. This approach extends the methodology previously outlined by Schnoebelen for WSTS. Furthermore, it establishes that the least fixed point of a monotone, continuous coverability relation within a Very-WSTS corresponds to the greatest inductive set, thereby generalizing Schnoebelen's earlier finding regarding WSTS.

This study introduces a novel method for analyzing the variability of active galactic nuclei (AGN) using a Bayesian framework. The approach employs a Gaussian process to model the light curve, with hyperparameters estimated via Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to derive posterior distributions. We developed a new Gaussian process kernel that incorporates a periodic component, allowing for the simultaneous modeling of both stochastic and periodic variations. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through simulations of synthetic light curves, which were then applied to real data from the Swift-BAT AGN sample. The resulting posterior distributions of the hyperparameters were used to characterize the variability of 100 AGN over a decade of observations. The findings reveal that the majority of these objects exhibit stochastic variability, with only a few showing periodic signals. Additionally, we calculated the power spectral density (PSD) for each AGN by fitting a power-law model to the PSD of the posterior predictive distribution. The resulting power-law indices were found to be consistent with those derived from traditional methods, which rely on the posterior mean of the light curve.

Quantum Darwinism offers a framework for understanding how objective classical reality emerges from quantum systems, a process driven by the redundancy of information. This study examines the emergence of objective reality within a spin-boson model, where a spin interacts with a bath of harmonic oscillators. We demonstrate that the information regarding the spin's state becomes redundantly encoded in subsets of the bath oscillators, a phenomenon that persists even when the spin-boson interaction is non-local. This finding indicates that the emergence of objective reality is not restricted to local interactions. Furthermore, we show that the information redundancy is robust against decoherence caused by interactions with an external environment. These results suggest that the emergence of objective reality is not only stable but also resilient to environmental disturbances.

This study introduces a novel method for estimating the reachable set of discrete-time dynamical systems by leveraging concepts from convex geometry, specifically convex bodies and ellipsoidal bounds. The approach utilizes a reachability analysis framework based on the evolution of convex bodies, which is then approximated through an iterative process involving ellipsoidal constraints. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this technique by applying it to a discrete-time model of a rigid body's attitude dynamics.

This study introduces SAINT, a novel model designed for tabular data problems, which integrates the strengths of tree-based methods and neural networks. By combining these two paradigms, SAINT achieves state-of-the-art performance across various benchmarks. The model's efficacy stems from its ability to learn from a diverse array of data subsets, thereby enhancing generalization. Empirical results indicate that SAINT surpasses traditional machine learning approaches and even outperforms current state-of-the-art deep learning techniques in several scenarios.

Transfer learning has become a standard approach for training machine learning models, particularly when labeled data is scarce. This technique leverages knowledge from a source domain to enhance performance in a target domain. However, its effectiveness relies heavily on the similarity between these domains; when they differ significantly, transfer learning can degrade performance. This paper introduces a novel method for selecting the most appropriate source domain to maximize the benefits of transfer learning. We propose a metric that quantifies the similarity between source and target domains by analyzing the distribution of their respective feature representations. This metric is then utilized to identify the optimal source domain for a given target. We validate our approach using a dataset of 10,000 images from the CIFAR-10 dataset as the target, paired with a collection of 100,000 images from various other datasets as potential sources. Our results demonstrate that the proposed metric effectively identifies the most suitable source domain, leading to superior transfer learning outcomes.

This study examines the chiral symmetry breaking transition within the framework of the mean-field approximation applied to the Polyakov loop extended Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model. We analyze the behavior of the chiral condensate and the constituent quark mass across varying temperatures and the strength of the gluonic background field. Furthermore, we evaluate the resulting equation of state and the speed of sound.

This study presents the initial direct search for dark matter in the $pp \to \chi\chi$ process, where $\chi$ represents a massive particle that subsequently decays into a $b$-quark pair. The analysis utilizes 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected by the ATLAS detector at the LHC's center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The search targets a mass range of 100 to 1,000 GeV for the dark matter particle, employing a simplified model featuring a vector mediator with a mass of 1 TeV. No significant excess beyond the Standard Model background is observed. Consequently, the 95% confidence level upper limit on the cross section for the $b\bar{b}$ channel is established at 0.13 pb for a dark matter mass of 100 GeV, which corresponds to a vector mediator coupling constant of approximately 0.01.

Locating concepts within software is a critical yet time-intensive task for developers. This paper introduces a new method that leverages crowd-sourced knowledge to enhance the efficiency of concept location. The proposed approach utilizes a crowd-based system to generate a ranked list of relevant code snippets, which developers can then examine to identify the target concept. We evaluated this method against two established techniques: traditional keyword search and the use of semantic similarity metrics. The results indicate that our proposed approach outperforms both existing methods.

This study introduces a block-diagonal preconditioner designed for the numerical solution of complex systems arising from the discretization of nonlinear Schrödinger equations. The preconditioner's effectiveness is demonstrated through its ability to accelerate the convergence of the GMRES method. The numerical experiments indicate that the preconditioner maintains robust performance across various scenarios, including those involving different nonlinearities and varying initial conditions.

This paper introduces a new approach to abstractive dialogue summarization that leverages discourse relations. We propose a model that integrates a discourse-aware encoder with a decoder, where the encoder utilizes a discourse-aware attention mechanism to capture the hierarchical structure of the conversation. The decoder is then trained to generate a summary that reflects the discourse relations of the input dialogue. Experiments conducted on the MultiWOZ 2.1 dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

This study introduces a deep learning approach for determining the Doppler broadening of nuclear cross-sections, utilizing the temperature-dependent resonance parameters of $^{235}$U as a case study. The method employs a neural network to map the relationship between resonance parameters and the resulting broadened cross-section. The network is trained on a dataset comprising 100,000 randomly selected resonance parameters, with each sample's input consisting of the resonance parameters and temperature, and the output being the corresponding broadened cross-section. The model's performance is validated against the standard SAMGRA code, demonstrating that the proposed technique achieves comparable accuracy while offering significantly faster computational speeds.

This paper presents a method for constructing $(n+1)$-pre-Lie algebras starting from $n$-pre-Lie algebras. Additionally, it establishes a correspondence between $n$-pre-Lie algebras and specific types of $n$-pre-Lie Yau algebras.

This study introduces a novel framework for managing real-time and non-real-time traffic in cellular networks, designed to enhance the quality of service for real-time users. The approach leverages the temporal characteristics of real-time traffic to boost the throughput of non-real-time users without compromising the Quality of Service (QoS) required by real-time users. The proposed scheme is evaluated against a simpler method that relies solely on the spatial properties of real-time traffic. The results demonstrate that the new scheme significantly outperforms the simpler method, increasing the throughput of non-real-time users by 10% to 20% while maintaining the necessary QoS for real-time traffic.

This study examines the approximation of entire functions of arbitrary finite order using their translates, $f(z+h)$, where $h$ is a complex parameter. We demonstrate that the Weierstrass approximation theorem fails in the uniform sense, though it holds true pointwise. Furthermore, we derive a specific estimate for the order of the approximating translates and establish that the theorem is stable under $L^p$ norms for $1 \le p \le \infty$.

The rheological behavior of disordered materials is significantly influenced by their microstructure, prompting the question of whether specific microstructural modifications can be made to achieve a desired rheological response. This study addresses that challenge by employing a discrete element model of a granular assembly to simulate the effects of various microstructural changes on the material's rheology. The results demonstrate that the material's rheological response can be effectively tuned through alterations in the microstructure, specifically by adjusting the distribution of contact forces and contact numbers.

Object detection is a critical capability for robotics and autonomous vehicles, where it must operate in dynamic, real-world settings. However, these applications often face a scarcity of labeled data, making continual learning essential for adapting to new environments. This study introduces a novel continual learning framework for object detection that utilizes a self-supervised approach to generate pseudo-labels for unlabeled data. By employing a self-supervised backbone, the method extracts features that are subsequently refined by a detection head to produce pseudo-labels. These labels are then used to train the detection head on new data while preserving knowledge from previous tasks. Experimental results on the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset demonstrate that this approach achieves superior performance compared to existing continual learning methods for object detection.

This study examines the production of quark-antiquark pairs within the framework of the Schwinger mechanism, specifically in the context of ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. We demonstrate that the medium-enhanced generation of these pairs becomes numerically significant only when the medium's temperature is sufficiently low.

This paper introduces DivCAM, a novel method for training neural networks to achieve domain generalization by leveraging the inherent diversity of unlabeled data. DivCAM operates by identifying and amplifying the most discriminative features within the model's feature space, thereby enhancing the model's ability to generalize across unseen domains. We demonstrate that DivCAM surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in domain generalization, particularly when applied to models trained on ImageNet and evaluated on the DomainNet benchmark.

This paper introduces a platform-independent blockchain designed to enhance the agent-based architecture of internet infrastructure. It outlines the blockchain's core principles and demonstrates its utility in securing and validating the interactions among autonomous agents.

This study examines the cosmological viability of both exponential and polynomial $\alpha$-attractor models, which are distinguished by their large-field inflationary potential. We analyze the inflationary dynamics of these models using the latest Planck 2018 cosmological data, specifically the 2018 release. Our findings indicate that the exponential $\alpha$-attractor model aligns more closely with observational data than the polynomial counterpart. Additionally, we explore the behavior of the tensor-to-scalar ratio within these frameworks, demonstrating that the polynomial model can be compatible with upcoming CMB experiments, such as LiteBIRD, whereas the exponential model may exceed the sensitivity limits of LiteBIRD.

This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the performance and accuracy of an end-to-end AI pipeline, specifically focusing on the impact of various optimization strategies. We demonstrate that significant gains—up to 100x in speed and 10% in accuracy—are achievable through careful optimization. Furthermore, we provide a detailed examination of the trade-offs between accuracy and performance, along with the specific architectural and algorithmic choices made to reach the final results.

This study evaluates the type 2 error rates of three distinct methods for concluding equivalence: the Bayes Factor, the Highest Density Interval (HDI) with Region of Practical Equivalence (ROPE), and frequentist equivalence tests. We assess these methods across various sample sizes and effect sizes, comparing their performance when calibrated to identical type 1 error rates. Results indicate that the Bayes Factor and HDI-ROPE approaches yield comparable type 2 error rates, which are consistently lower than those of frequentist equivalence tests. Furthermore, the Bayes Factor demonstrates superior performance in terms of type 2 error rates when calibrated to the same type 1 error rates compared to the HDI-ROPE method.

This paper introduces a digital semantic communication framework that integrates adversarial training to enhance the quality of received images. The system employs a semantic encoder to extract features from source images and a semantic decoder to reconstruct these images. To improve robustness, adversarial training is applied to the semantic decoder, which simultaneously optimizes the semantic encoder. The resulting adversarial semantic communication system (ASCS) is evaluated using the CUB-200-2011 dataset. The findings demonstrate that the ASCS achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, particularly in terms of received image quality.

Frameworks like Reshape, which utilize data reshaping, are increasingly popular for addressing skew in data processing. However, these tools often fail to provide a clear explanation of their internal operations, leaving users uncertain about the specific mechanisms used to mitigate skew. This paper introduces a formal model for data reshaping, which serves to clarify the process and enable the development of verification tools. We have developed a Verilog-based formal checker grounded in this model to validate the correctness of Reshape's implementation. Our evaluation demonstrates that this formal checker successfully identifies bugs in Reshape, including a critical flaw that could result in data loss.

This paper examines the information loss incurred when moving from a comonad or from an adjunction to a resulting modal interior operator. We demonstrate that this loss can be quantified using a specific measure of information, which is defined as a coproduct of the relevant coalgebras.

This study introduces a novel graphical Chinese restaurant process (GCPR) designed to enhance the Bayesian inference of network autoregressive models. By leveraging the GCPR, we develop a new prior that effectively captures both the local and global dependencies inherent in network structures. We subsequently apply this prior to construct a Bayesian framework for network autoregressive models, demonstrating its utility in analyzing data from a social media platform.

This paper introduces SciFact, a novel dataset designed for verifying scientific claims. It comprises 10,000 claims from Wikipedia articles, each paired with a supporting or refuting sentence from a relevant source. To address the scarcity of labeled data in scientific domains, we developed a semi-supervised approach that leverages a large collection of unlabeled scientific claims. This method utilizes a pre-trained language model to generate pseudo-labels, which are subsequently refined through a self-training process. Experimental results indicate that our semi-supervised framework significantly outperforms existing baselines, demonstrating the viability of applying semi-supervised learning to scientific claim verification.

This study introduces a novel approach to segment the posterior eye section in both healthy and pathological scans, utilizing a deep learning framework that integrates a U-Net architecture with a novel attention mechanism. The proposed method effectively isolates the posterior segment by leveraging the inherent characteristics of the input data. Experimental results demonstrate that this technique outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior accuracy in both segmentation and classification tasks.

Cognitive models frequently rely on the assumption that parameters remain static or homogeneous, yet this premise often fails to capture the temporal dynamics inherent in cognitive processes. This study introduces a Bayesian framework for estimating time-varying parameters within a sequential sampling model, utilizing a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach to infer these fluctuations. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through its application to a sequential sampling model, with results indicating that the proposed framework can effectively recover time-varying parameters from simulated data.
This study presents a novel criterion for determining Mersenne compositeness, which relies on the Jacobi symbol $\left(\frac{2}{q}\right)$ and the rank of apparition of 2 modulo $q$.
We examine the impact of dispersive dominance and dissipation rate saturation on the Boltzmann equation within the context of hydrodynamics.

We present a study of the [C II] 158 $\mu$m and [C III] 1900 $\mu$m emission lines in 11 extreme starburst galaxies, utilizing data from the Herschel Space Observatory. Our analysis reveals that the ratios of [C II] to [C III] emission are significantly higher in these starbursts than in normal star-forming galaxies. This enhancement is attributed to the presence of low-density molecular winds or circumgalactic gas reservoirs, which facilitate the conversion of [C II] emission into [C III] emission. Furthermore, we observe a strong correlation between the [C II]/[C III] ratios and the specific star formation rate (SFR) surface density, indicating that the elevated ratios are driven by the intense star formation activity typical of these extreme starbursts.

This study introduces a new method for annotating spoken utterances that are both interrogative and declarative. The approach involves a two-stage process: first, annotators independently label the data, and second, they review each other's work to identify and resolve discrepancies. We demonstrate that this collaborative model significantly enhances inter-annotator agreement compared to single-stage labeling. Furthermore, we show that annotator performance improves as they gain experience through the iterative process. The paper also outlines the specific challenges involved in creating a high-quality dataset for this task and presents the resulting data, which is publicly available.

We present a new analysis of the timescales for inner disc dispersal in young stellar objects (YSOs) using the ALMA survey of the Ophiuchus star-forming region. This study examines 100 Class I and Class II YSOs, focusing on their millimetre-sized dust rings. By applying a novel method to determine the inner disc edge, we derived the timescales for inner disc dispersal. Our findings reveal a strong correlation between stellar mass and inner-disc lifetime, with more massive stars hosting longer-lived discs. Additionally, we observed a significant link between the inner-disc lifetime and the disc's outer radius. These results align with the hypothesis that inner-disc dispersal is driven by photoevaporation, which is more efficient in massive stars due to their higher ionizing photon output.

This study introduces a novel approach to enhance the accuracy of the discontinuous Galerkin (DG) method by selectively modifying its coefficients. The proposed technique targets the numerical dissipation inherent in the standard DG method, which is most pronounced in high-frequency regions. By adjusting these coefficients, the method achieves greater accuracy without compromising stability. The paper details the specific modifications applied to the coefficients and provides a thorough analysis of the resulting numerical dissipation. Furthermore, the method's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical experiments.

This study examines the residue behaviors of a polaron within a Bose gas situated in a double-well potential. We demonstrate that the repulsive nature of the Bose gas significantly impacts these residue behaviors, a finding that is substantiated by numerical simulations.

This study introduces a Markov chain framework designed to model the logistics of prepositioning relief supplies ahead of potential hurricanes. The model tracks the movement of these items between inland storage facilities and coastal shelters, accounting for the stochastic nature of hurricane landfalls. By analyzing the steady-state behavior of this system, the research identifies the optimal number of items to store at inland locations to ensure that a specific target probability of meeting demand at coastal sites is achieved.

We introduce a new approximate analytic formula for the gravitational wave background produced by compact binaries, which is derived from the ensemble-averaged gravitational wave spectrum of individual binaries. This approach is validated against numerical simulations and compared with existing methods. Our results demonstrate that the formula achieves accuracy comparable to other techniques, with the added benefit of being significantly more straightforward to implement. Furthermore, we apply this formula to analyze the impact of upcoming Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments on the detection of stochastic gravitational waves from cosmological first-order phase transitions. We find that the sensitivity of PTAs to the amplitude of such signals is largely independent of the specific spectral shape. Additionally, we show that the sensitivity to the duration of the phase transition is highly dependent on the spectral shape, and we discuss the implications of these findings for constraining the properties of such cosmological events.

This paper examines Bayesian coordination games where agents must select a shared action from a set of multiple equilibria. We demonstrate that agents can successfully coordinate on a specific equilibrium even without knowing the exact distribution of types, provided they possess a "robust" prior belief regarding the types of other agents. This finding holds true regardless of whether agents have complete or only partial information about their own types.

This study introduces a novel terahertz spectroscopy method for aqueous solutions, utilizing a coplanar waveguide (CPW) integrated with a microfluidic channel. The CPW, fabricated on a silicon substrate, is engineered to function as a resonator at room temperature, with its resonance frequency precisely tuned by the microfluidic channel's dimensions. This configuration enables the simultaneous measurement of both the real and imaginary components of the complex permittivity of liquids. The technique was validated using water, ethanol, and a mixture of water and ethanol, with the resulting permittivity values aligning well with established literature data.

This study introduces a novel framework for forecasting the risk of contagion spread in urban environments. The approach integrates environmental and human activity variables to enhance predictive accuracy. The model is constructed using a Bayesian network, which is trained via a hybrid algorithm combining particle filtering and Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. The proposed framework is evaluated using a dataset from the 2017 Urban Challenge, which includes data from 100,000 individuals across 100,000 locations in the United Kingdom. The results demonstrate that the model effectively predicts contagion risk and can be adapted to various scenarios by incorporating different environmental and human activity variables.

This study introduces a multi-resolution Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) framework designed to address the challenges of high-density ratio scenarios. The approach employs a multi-phase model to manage voids and phase separation, alongside a new artificial viscosity formulation that ensures stability in high-density contrasts. Additionally, a particle shifting technique is implemented to mitigate particle clustering. The proposed method is validated through several numerical tests, including the Rayleigh-Taylor instability, the Rayleigh-Bénard convection, and the interaction of a water droplet with a gas jet.

Nodal lines in momentum space represent one-dimensional loops of band degeneracy that are protected by symmetry. These lines are typically characterized by a one-dimensional topological invariant known as the Wilson loop. In this study, we introduce a new class of materials featuring two distinct nodal lines that are linked together. We demonstrate that the topology of this linked configuration is governed by a two-dimensional invariant, specifically the linking number. Furthermore, we show that the presence of these linked nodal lines can be detected through the emergence of a higher-order topological surface state.

The development of event generator tools for high-luminosity physics experiments is becoming increasingly complex, as the growing number of rare processes and the heightened sensitivity to background noise demand greater computational efficiency. To address this, we introduce a new software framework designed to accelerate Monte Carlo event generation. This system leverages the high performance of modern GPUs by utilizing their massive parallel processing capabilities. The core of the software is a C++ implementation of the Pythia 8 event generator, which has been adapted to run on GPUs. This adaptation involves rewriting the event generation and parton shower algorithms to execute in parallel, as well as optimizing the software for GPU execution. The resulting GPU-accelerated Pythia 8 software has been benchmarked against the original CPU-based version, demonstrating a significant performance gain.

This study examines the characteristics of mean-type mappings through the lens of their invariant means. We introduce a novel class of mappings, termed $G$-monotonic mean-type mappings, which generalize both monotonic and geometric-mean-type mappings. Furthermore, we establish that the composition of two $G$-monotonic mappings remains $G$-monotonic. The paper also explores the invariant means associated with these mappings and provides a characterization of the invariant means for the specific case of $G$-monotonic $m$-means.

This study presents a new analysis of the molecular gas distribution in the outer Galaxy, utilizing the 12CO(1-0) line emission data from the IRAM 30m telescope. The dataset covers a region extending from approximately 10 to 18 kpc from the Galactic center, with a resolution of 1.5 degrees. The research compares the observed molecular gas distribution against that of HI gas, as well as against the distributions of atomic and molecular gas derived from the 21-cm line and 13CO(1-0) emission, respectively. The analysis reveals that the observed molecular gas distribution aligns well with the HI gas distribution, whereas the 13CO(1-0) emission shows a significant discrepancy. The study further examines the relationship between the 13CO(1-0) emission and the 12CO(1-0) emission, finding that the 13CO(1-0) emission is generally weaker than expected based on the 12CO(1-0) emission. The authors conclude that the 13CO(1-0) emission is likely due to the presence of a significant amount of molecular gas that is not detected in the 13CO(1-0) emission. This paper introduces a consumer choice game designed to examine wage redistribution. The model features a continuum of consumers who select between two firms, each offering a distinct wage. The resulting consumer distribution is then analyzed to determine the equilibrium outcomes.

This study examines the dynamical behavior of an active glass characterized by a combination of repulsive interactions and quenched disorder, incorporating an alignment mechanism that governs the orientation of active forces. We demonstrate that this alignment interaction drives a transition from a glassy state to a fluid state, a process marked by a sudden shift in dynamical properties. Furthermore, we identify a distinct regime where alignment induces a dynamic arrest, resulting in a glassy phase that is more rigid than the original system.

u_e)$. This enhancement is attributed to the significant contribution of the $	au$ lepton's mass within the $\mathcal{B}_{cc}$ system. Furthermore, we calculate the branching fractions for these decays and find that they are comparable to those of the analogous mesonic decays.

This study introduces a novel game called "Locate," designed to assess how well humans can identify their own positions within a 2D space. In this game, participants, referred to as "Locators," attempt to determine their location based on visual cues. To evaluate the Locators' performance, we trained a machine learning model using the Locators' data to predict its own position. The model's accuracy was then compared against that of the top human Locators. Results indicate that the most effective model achieved a success rate of 80%, surpassing the best human Locators, who succeeded in only 60% of cases. Additionally, we examined the model's ability to predict the locations of "blind" Locators—those who had not yet made a move. The model demonstrated a 90% success rate in these instances, suggesting it can effectively anticipate the positions of Locators who have not yet acted.

This study introduces a novel approach to frequency band selection for machinery monitoring that leverages the Band Relevance Factor (BRF). Unlike conventional methods that rely on fixed thresholds or arbitrary criteria, this technique utilizes a specific metric to identify bands containing the most significant fault-related information. The proposed method was validated through a case study involving a gearbox with a localized crack, demonstrating its effectiveness in isolating critical fault signatures.

This study examines the superconducting properties of CaPtSi$_3$ and CaIrSi$_3$ using resistivity, specific heat, and magnetization measurements. The results indicate that both materials exhibit bulk superconductivity with transition temperatures of 2.5 K and 2.8 K, respectively. The superconducting coherence lengths are estimated at approximately 100 nm for CaPtSi$_3$ and 200 nm for CaIrSi$_3$. Furthermore, the specific heat data for both compounds aligns well with a two-band superconducting model.

The Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation serves as a cornerstone in optimal control theory, yet its solution via standard numerical techniques is severely constrained by the curse of dimensionality. This study introduces a novel approach to approximating the HJB equation using a deep neural network, where the network's parameters are optimized by minimizing a loss function derived from the HJB equation itself. The proposed method is validated through numerical experiments on two distinct control problems, demonstrating its efficacy.

Quantum computing holds the potential to significantly enhance various machine learning algorithms, including supervised classification methods. This study introduces a quantum approach for supervised classification that leverages the quantum kernel method. We demonstrate that this technique can be implemented using a quantum circuit with a depth of only one, making it highly suitable for execution on near-term quantum hardware.

This paper introduces a multi-layered energy modeling framework designed to enhance the control strategies of electric power systems. The proposed approach integrates a high-fidelity model with a low-fidelity model, where the latter is refined using data-driven techniques. The study demonstrates the application of this framework in the context of a heat exchanger, showing how it facilitates the development of more effective control strategies.

This study introduces a deep learning methodology for analyzing percolation states, specifically to determine key features such as densities and correlation lengths. The approach utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on simulated percolation data to classify states as either percolating or non-percolating. The network's output is then processed using a support vector machine (SVM) to extract quantitative metrics. The proposed technique is validated by applying it to both simulated and experimental data, demonstrating its effectiveness in analyzing percolation characteristics.

This study introduces a novel method for measuring temperature within a reactor by analyzing the temperature-dependent shift in proton resonance frequency. The approach utilizes a 1.5 T NMR spectrometer, where a 100 mL sample of water is placed inside a 100 mm diameter cylindrical reactor. This study examines the impact of inhomogeneity and randomness on superconducting fluctuations close to the transition point in disordered superconductors. We demonstrate that the random distribution of the superconducting order parameter's magnitude and phase can be effectively modeled using a stochastic Ginzburg-Landau framework. By applying the renormalization group method, we derive the critical exponents for the correlation length and the correlation volume. Our findings indicate that these exponents remain unaffected by inhomogeneity and randomness, provided the system is situated within the weak disorder regime.

This study examines the IEEE 802.15.4 UWB physical layer to determine how its configuration influences indoor localization services. We analyze the impact of different physical layer settings on the reliability and energy consumption of these services, utilizing a realistic indoor environment. The findings indicate that while the physical layer can be adjusted to meet specific reliability and energy constraints, the resulting performance is highly dependent on the specific indoor environment.

This paper presents an algorithm capable of $k$-median clustering for finite point sets in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with a fixed approximation ratio, provided that $k$ and $d$ are treated as constants. The method relies on a novel, efficient approach to enumerating all $k$-median centers that are optimal for a specific subset of the data.

This study introduces a double averaging approach for multi-agent reinforcement learning (RL) to enhance the convergence of distributed algorithms. The proposed scheme employs the average of the most recent policy parameters as the reference point for updating the average policy, while simultaneously using the average of the most recent value function estimates to update the average value function. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that this method achieves a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ for both the average policy and value function, where $T$ represents the number of iterations. Furthermore, numerical experiments confirm that this double averaging technique outperforms existing methods in terms of convergence speed.

This paper presents a coalgebraic $\mu$-calculus that eliminates the need for guardedness transformations, thereby permitting unguarded formulas. We demonstrate that the semantics of this calculus correspond to a coalgebraic version of the $\mu$-calculus, which is defined through a specific coalgebraic functor.

This study introduces a novel methodology for pinpointing heat sources within a three-dimensional domain using sparse temperature readings from a two-dimensional surface. We employ a hierarchical Bayesian framework to estimate the spatial distribution of heat sources, which facilitates the integration of prior knowledge regarding their locations and magnitudes. To address the computational challenges inherent in Bayesian inference for this problem, we utilize a variational approach. This method is designed to be efficient and scalable, making it suitable for handling large-scale scenarios. We validate the approach through numerical experiments, demonstrating its efficacy in recovering heat sources across various configurations.

This study introduces a novel approach to imputing air quality data by leveraging the correlation between vehicle trajectories and pollutant concentrations. The method involves selecting optimal vehicle paths for each missing data point and employing a deep learning model to predict the corresponding pollutant levels. The path selection process is formulated as a combinatorial optimization challenge, solved using a deep reinforcement learning algorithm. The model's predictive capability is evaluated across three pollutants—NO2, CO, and PM10—using data from the City of Barcelona. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, with the performance gain directly linked to the quality of the selected vehicle paths.

This paper investigates the unitary group $U$ linked to the group $SL_*(2, A_n)$, where $n \geq 2$. We demonstrate that the structural composition of $U$ can be characterized through its linear representations.

This paper introduces a novel approach to automatically generating background music for persuasive videos. We propose a new metric for evaluating the effectiveness of such videos, which incorporates the impact of background music on the viewer's experience. To achieve this, we developed a system that creates music dynamically based on the video's content. Our method utilizes a pre-trained deep neural network to analyze the video and extract a set of content-related features. These features are then mapped to corresponding musical attributes, which are used to generate the background track. We conducted experiments using a dataset of 100 persuasive videos, each paired with a generated background song. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly enhances the persuasiveness of the videos.

This study examines the quantum dynamics of a trapped ion system, where the ion is confined by a harmonic potential and coupled to a quantized electromagnetic field. We demonstrate that the classical Hamiltonian function, representing the system's total energy, can be expressed as the expectation value of the quantum Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we show that the time evolution of this classical Hamiltonian adheres to Hamilton's equations.

Neuroscience models are frequently characterized by numerous parameters, making it essential to pinpoint specific regions within the parameter space that accurately reflect the system's behavior. This study introduces a novel method for estimating the probability density function of these parameters using a Bayesian framework. The approach employs a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to generate samples from the posterior distribution, which is derived by combining a likelihood function with a prior distribution. The likelihood function is constructed based on the discrepancy between model predictions and experimental data, while the prior distribution incorporates existing knowledge about the parameters. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through its application to a Hodgkin-Huxley model, where it successfully identified the parameter space consistent with observed neuronal firing patterns.

This paper introduces Camouflage Fusion Learning (CFL), a framework designed to enhance instance segmentation by leveraging the complementary strengths of various existing models. The core of CFL is a Camouflage Fusion Module (CFM), which integrates features from multiple networks to create a unified representation. This approach enables the model to capture diverse object attributes, such as texture, color, and shape, thereby improving segmentation accuracy. The CFM is built upon a lightweight, efficient architecture that supports the integration of numerous networks without compromising computational efficiency. Extensive experiments on the MS-COCO dataset demonstrate that CFL achieves state-of-the-art performance, with a 2.0 mAP improvement over the strongest baseline. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChengBi1995/CFL.

This study examines the impact of Lorentz-violating tensors on the coherence length within the framework of the Ginzburg-Landau theory. We demonstrate that these tensors can either increase or decrease the coherence length, contingent upon the specific values of the system's parameters.

This paper introduces a novel approach to identifying and correcting bias in AI models by leveraging the insights of human experts. The proposed method operates in two stages: first, it utilizes the expert's input to pinpoint specific groups within the dataset that are likely to be underrepresented in the model's predictions. Second, it employs these identified groups to generate new training data, thereby enhancing the model's performance. The authors validate this framework using a real-world dataset of job postings, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting and mitigating bias.

This paper introduces R(Det)$^2$, a novel framework for object detection that leverages the synergy between detection and regression tasks. The method employs a shared backbone to generate feature maps, which are then processed by two distinct branches: a detection branch utilizing anchor-based Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) and a regression branch applying a NMS-free algorithm. The core innovation lies in a new loss function that facilitates bidirectional information flow between these branches. Specifically, the detection branch's predictions refine the regression targets, while the regression branch's outputs enhance the detection anchors. This mutual enhancement mechanism allows the model to effectively utilize complementary information from both tasks, resulting in superior performance. Extensive testing on the MS-COCO 2017 dataset demonstrates that R(Det)$^2$ outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 2.0% improvement in AP with ResNet-50 and a 2.3% improvement with ResNet-101.

Adversarial training has become a standard approach for enhancing the robustness of deep neural networks. However, recent research indicates that applying adversarial training to small input perturbations fails to yield significant robustness improvements. This study demonstrates that zeroing out small input gradients effectively neutralizes FGSM attacks, thereby rendering adversarial training ineffective. We further reveal that this vulnerability stems from the fact that the FGSM attack is invariant to the addition of small, constant values to the input. To address this, we propose a novel attack method that incorporates a small, constant input perturbation, which successfully bypasses the limitations of existing FGSM-based defenses.

We examine the Thakurta metric, a spherically symmetric solution to the Einstein field equations that describes a black hole with a time-dependent mass. This metric is often cited as a potential model for primordial black holes (PBHs) formed from the collapse of overdense regions in the early universe. However, we demonstrate that the Thakurta metric fails to represent a physically realistic PBH formation scenario. Specifically, we show that existing constraints on PBH abundance derived from the lack of observed gravitational lensing remain valid.

This study examines the stability of optimization dynamics under switching signals, specifically within the context of convex optimization. We demonstrate that the average dwell time of the switching signal is a critical factor in determining the convergence of these dynamics. Furthermore, we establish that the switching signal's average dwell time dictates the rate at which the objective function value decreases.

Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables the secure outsourcing of computations to untrusted servers, yet current FHE implementations on CPUs remain too slow for practical use. This paper introduces BTS, a specialized architecture designed to accelerate FHE computations. BTS achieves a 1000-fold speedup over CPUs by utilizing a custom instruction set and a dedicated hardware accelerator. The architecture employs a novel instruction set that streamlines FHE operations, alongside a hardware accelerator built on a systolic array to execute these instructions in parallel. Furthermore, BTS incorporates a memory hierarchy optimized for FHE data, which reduces data movement and enhances bandwidth efficiency. Experimental results indicate that BTS outperforms CPUs by a factor of 1000 in execution time while maintaining a 100-fold improvement in memory bandwidth.

This study examines a specific random matrix ensemble defined by a determinant formula involving a Hankel determinant of moments. We demonstrate that the spectral correlation functions for this ensemble can be expressed using a specific class of orthogonal polynomials. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the $n$-th orthogonal polynomial and establish its asymptotic behavior in the large $n$ limit.

Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers within diamond are promising candidates for quantum information applications, particularly in sensing and quantum memory. This study demonstrates that the NV center's spin state can be read out via a single-photon Raman transition, which is subsequently detected through fluorescence. We show that the resulting Raman signal is highly sensitive to the spin state and can be modulated by varying the frequency of the laser. Furthermore, we propose a method to generate entanglement between two NV centers using a single-photon Raman transition.

In 1976, Bell demonstrated that the factorizability condition is a necessary consequence of local causality, a derivation that relied on the assumption of a causal ordering between the measurement events. This paper examines the derivation of factorizability from local causality within the context of spacelike-separated measurements, arguing that the condition remains necessary even when no specific causal order is presupposed.

This study introduces a new framework for generating continuous video motion, designed to overcome the limitations of existing methods that rely on discrete, frame-by-frame representations. Our approach utilizes positional embeddings to create a continuous motion model, which is then trained using a novel loss function to ensure the resulting outputs are temporally smooth. We demonstrate that this method produces high-quality, temporally coherent videos and outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques.

This study extends the $\chi$-correspondence originally defined by I. M. Isaacs, which maps character degrees to character degrees. We demonstrate that this correspondence maintains a direct link between the degrees of distinct irreducible characters. Furthermore, we establish that the correspondence maps the degrees of irreducible characters of a subgroup $H$ within a group $G$ to specific subsets of the corresponding character degrees of $G$.

This study introduces a deep learning approach for estimating radiation dose and date from measured signals. The method utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) to process raw detector data, delivering simultaneous predictions for dose and date. The model was trained using a dataset comprising 1,000 measurements from a plastic scintillator detector, which included 500 samples from a $^{137}$Cs source and 500 background samples. The network was evaluated on a separate test set of 1,000 measurements, consisting of 500 background samples and 500 samples from a $^{60}$Co source. The results demonstrate that the proposed technique achieves high accuracy in both date and dose estimation, even when the source is unknown.

This paper investigates the existence of solutions for a class of nonlocal problems featuring nonstandard growth, formulated as:
$$
\begin{cases}
-\mathrm{div}(|\nabla u|^{p(x)-2}\nabla u+|\nabla u|^{q(x)-2}\nabla u)+\lambda|u|^{p(x)-2}u+\mu|u|^{p(x)-2}u+\delta|u|^{p(x)-2}u=0, & \text{in } \Omega, \\
u=0, & \text{on } \partial\Omega,
\end{cases}
$$
where $\Omega$ is a bounded domain in $\mathbb{R}^N$, $\lambda, \mu, \delta$ are positive constants, and $p, q$ are continuous variable exponents. We establish the existence of solutions by applying the Mountain Pass Theorem within Sobolev spaces defined by variable exponents, thereby extending previous findings that relied on constant exponents.

The modulation transfer function (MTF) serves as a standard metric for evaluating detector performance, yet its calculation is often hindered by the scarcity of experimental data. This paper introduces a method to derive the MTF from a single image of a point source, utilizing a neural network trained on simulated data. The approach was validated using a simulated point source image from a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) and successfully applied to a real-world image of a point source captured by a CMOS camera.

LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) is a widely adopted technique for elucidating the behavior of opaque machine learning models. However, it suffers from a lack of theoretical guarantees and can produce inconsistent results. This paper introduces S-LIME, a novel approach that integrates a statistical framework to ensure both consistency and interpretability. S-LIME generates explanations by fitting a local linear model to a synthetic dataset derived from the original model's predictions. This synthetic data is constructed by sampling from a Gaussian distribution centered at the input point, with a covariance matrix determined by the Hessian of the local linear model. Theoretically, we demonstrate that S-LIME is consistent under mild assumptions, and we provide a closed-form solution for the optimal perturbation distribution. Empirical evaluations on various datasets confirm that S-LIME outperforms existing methods in both consistency and interpretability.

This study introduces a Bayesian convolutional neural network (CNN) designed to enhance the accuracy of image classification. The model's performance is refined through feedback from human annotators, who evaluate the system's predictions and provide corrections. This iterative process of prediction and correction is repeated until the model achieves satisfactory results. The proposed approach is evaluated on the MNIST dataset, demonstrating that it outperforms both standard CNNs and Bayesian CNNs lacking human feedback.

This study examines the magnetic fluctuations of the spin-liquid compound $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$ using inelastic neutron scattering. We demonstrate that the observed low-energy magnetic excitations are well described by a two-dimensional (2D) Kitaev model incorporating nearest-neighbor spin-orbit coupling. Specifically, the low-lying crystal-field (CF) states are identified as the primary source of these magnetic fluctuations. Furthermore, we observe that the CF levels are highly sensitive to the spin-orbit coupling strength, which in turn dictates the nature of the magnetic fluctuations.

This paper examines the blow-down limits of entire convex translating solutions to the mean curvature flow. We demonstrate that in two dimensions, taking the limit as $h \to \infty$ for the rescaled solution $e^{-hT}X(t+h, \cdot)$ yields a blow-down of the entire convex translating solution to a half-line. In three dimensions, we establish that the same blow-down process for $e^{-hT}X(t+h, \cdot)$ results in a blow-down of the entire convex translating solution in $\mathbb{R}^3$ to a half-line.

This study introduces Weight Fixation, a mechanism designed to enhance the training of neural networks. By automatically identifying and locking weights that have converged to stable values, the method reduces computational costs and accelerates the training process. We demonstrate that Weight Fixation is compatible with various optimization algorithms, including SGD, Adam, and Nesterov's accelerated gradient. Furthermore, the approach is versatile, functioning effectively across different architectures such as CNNs, RNNs, and Transformers, as well as diverse tasks like image classification, machine translation, and question answering.

This study introduces DeepCluE, a framework designed to perform unsupervised image clustering by leveraging both instance-level and cluster-level contrastive learning. The method employs a two-stage process: initially, it trains a feature extractor using instance-level contrastive learning, followed by a clustering phase that utilizes cluster-level contrastive learning to refine the results. Experimental evaluations on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrate that DeepCluE achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

This paper introduces a new process algebra, contrasim, designed to support bisimulation-based checking of contrasimilarity. We demonstrate that contrasimilarity constitutes a precongruence for the underlying algebraic structure and that bisimulation equivalence within contrasim aligns precisely with bisimulation equivalence in the original process system.

This paper introduces the notion of stringor bundles, which function as the natural extension of spinor bundles and spin^c bundles. We establish that every stringor bundle corresponds to a specific Lie group, which serves as the associated structure group. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the stringor bundle is the universal bundle for principal stringor reductions.

This study examines the propagation of ion-acoustic solitary waves within a magnetized plasma environment characterized by the presence of both nonthermal electrons and positrons. The analysis employs the standard nonlinear Schrödinger equation to determine the conditions under which the plasma system exhibits modulational instability. The findings indicate that the plasma system is modulationally unstable when the coefficient of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation is positive. Furthermore, the paper derives the analytical expression for ion-acoustic solitary waves and their corresponding potential, subsequently validating these theoretical results through numerical simulations.

This study examines the parametric decay of Alfvén waves into a slow mode and an ion cyclotron wave within a magnetized plasma. We derive a set of coupled equations describing the evolution of these three modes and analyze their solutions under the assumption of a constant pump amplitude. The analysis reveals that the instability can be triggered when the pump Alfvén wave possesses a sufficiently large amplitude and its frequency is close to the sum of the frequencies of the slow mode and the ion cyclotron wave. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the growth rate of this instability is significantly enhanced by the presence of a background magnetic field.

We present a novel method to determine the fragmentation scale of a molecular cloud filament by analyzing the ratio of the filament's width to its length. This approach relies on the premise that the filament's width is governed by ambipolar diffusion, which operates at a specific scale. This scale is identified as the point where the filament's mass per unit length equals the critical mass for gravitational collapse. This critical mass is derived from the virial theorem, incorporating both magnetic and thermal pressures. The resulting formula for the fragmentation scale depends on the filament's width, the cloud's magnetic field strength, and the cloud's temperature. This theoretical framework is validated using numerical simulations of a magnetized filament. Furthermore, we apply this method to observations of the L183 filament, which exhibits a width of 0.03 pc and a length of 0.15 pc. The analysis indicates that the filament's fragmentation scale is approximately 0.02 pc, a value consistent with the observed spacing of its cores.

This study examines the dynamics of a two-level system coupled to its environment, specifically analyzing how the initial state influences the system's evolution. We demonstrate that altering the prepared state can lead to variations in the decay rates. Furthermore, we show that the system's evolution is not necessarily monotonic, as the decay rate can fluctuate over time.

This study examines the impact of measurement-induced decoherence on a two-level system, specifically focusing on the role of spin-lattice interactions. We demonstrate that regardless of the measurement basis orientation, varying the spin-lattice interaction induces quantum coherence. Furthermore, we show that the measurement basis orientation can be determined by analyzing the behavior of coherence as a function of spin-lattice interactions.

This paper introduces a priority-based goal planning approach designed to prevent deadlocks in multi-agent navigation. The method assigns priorities to agents based on their proximity to goals, thereby resolving conflicts and ensuring deadlock-free movement. We demonstrate that the approach guarantees collision-free navigation for any number of agents and any graph topology, provided the graph is connected. Furthermore, we prove that the method is optimal regarding the total number of agent moves. The study also examines the computational complexity of the algorithm and evaluates its performance through simulations.

This paper introduces CARLANE, a novel dataset designed to advance research in lane detection. It features 1,000 images captured from a vehicle traveling on highways and roads, annotated with precise pixel-level lane markings. The collection includes diverse scenarios such as day and night conditions, varying weather states, and both straight and curved road sections. To facilitate the development of robust models, the dataset is split into training, validation, and testing subsets. We also provide baseline results using the YOLOv4 algorithm, which achieved an mAP of 0.70 on the test set.

This study examines the contact line behavior of water drops resting on a hydrogel surface, specifically focusing on the influence of adsorbed particles. We demonstrate that these particles significantly enhance the pinning force at the contact line. This phenomenon is attributed to the formation of a capillary bridge between the particle and the substrate, which generates a substantial pinning force. Furthermore, we analyze the relationship between the pinning force and the particle's contact angle, revealing that the maximum pinning force occurs when the particle is in a partially wet state.

This study examines the impact of missing nodes on social network analysis within the context of student collaboration. We demonstrate that absent nodes can significantly skew correlation calculations, leading to erroneous conclusions regarding the relationships between students. To address this, we propose a method for imputing missing nodes in collaboration networks, which subsequently enhances the accuracy of correlation estimates.

This study introduces a novel approach for estimating wind velocity by integrating the Maximum Entropy Method (MEM) with Autoregressive (AR) modeling. The primary objective is to derive accurate wind speed estimates from brief time-series data, thereby enhancing the precision of wind resource assessments. The proposed methodology was validated using data from the 100 m tower at the NREL Wind Energy Technology Center in Boulder, Colorado. The results demonstrate that this technique yields superior wind speed estimates compared to conventional methods.

This study presents the first comprehensive analysis of the chemical abundances for Ruprecht 147 and UBC 274, two newly identified open clusters. Utilizing high-resolution, high signal-to-noise spectra from the Keck/HIRES and VLT/UVES instruments, we measured the abundances of 14 elements (H, He, C, N, O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, Ca, Ti, Cr, Fe, and Ni) in both clusters. Our findings reveal that UBC 274 is significantly more metal-rich than Ruprecht 147, with a metallicity difference of approximately 0.2 dex. Furthermore, we determined that the age of UBC 274 is roughly 100 million years, whereas Ruprecht 147 is approximately 200 million years old. These results indicate that UBC 274 is younger and more metal-rich, suggesting that the two clusters likely formed from distinct parent molecular clouds.

This paper introduces a method for enhancing neural machine translation (NMT) by leveraging a semantic equivalence classifier. The approach involves training a classifier to identify whether pairs of sentences are semantically equivalent, followed by using this model to filter the NMT decoder's output candidates. This filtering process ensures that only semantically equivalent sentences are retained. Our experiments demonstrate that this method significantly improves translation quality, achieving a BLEU score increase of 1.0 on the WMT14 English-to-German task and 1.2 on the WMT14 English-to-French task.

We introduce a novel approach to detect entanglement transitions in monitored open quantum many-body systems. This method relies on the observation that the variance of the number of unmeasured qubits within a subsystem serves as a sensitive marker for these transitions. We demonstrate that this variance can be efficiently computed using a matrix product operator (MPO) representation. Furthermore, we show that the associated entanglement transition can be characterized by a critical value of the variance, which remains finite in the thermodynamic limit.

This study introduces a tight-binding model for the spin-orbit coupling within transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) monolayers, specifically addressing the spin-dependent electronic properties of MoS$_2$ and WS$_2$. By incorporating the spin-orbit coupling of the constituent atoms, the model elucidates the distinct spin behaviors observed in these systems. Furthermore, the model is utilized to calculate the spin-orbit splitting energy for TMD monolayers, demonstrating strong agreement with experimental data.

Quantum reservoir computing (QRc) is a machine learning technique that leverages the nonlinear dynamics of quantum systems to forecast future states. This study examines the theoretical foundations of QRc by analyzing how its various representations relate to the echo state property (ESP) and fading memory property (FMP). We demonstrate that the ESP and FMP are applicable to both the Schrödinger and Heisenberg pictures, with the latter offering a more straightforward approach to calculating the reservoir computing kernel. Furthermore, we establish that the kernel of a quantum reservoir is defined by the correlation between the reservoir's initial state and its evolved state. Finally, we illustrate that the kernel of a quantum reservoir can be expressed as a sum of kernels from multiple classical reservoirs.

This study examines the evanescent-field trapping of atoms within microrings, specifically analyzing the impact of high-order modes on the trapping potential. We demonstrate that incorporating these modes significantly lowers the power needed to create a potential well, thereby enabling the use of smaller, more compact devices. Furthermore, we investigate the influence of microring geometry on the trapping potential and the resulting atom wavefunction. Our findings indicate that the potential landscape is highly sensitive to the ring's dimensions, with the potential well's depth and the wavefunction's spatial extent being particularly responsive to changes in the ring's radius.

This study examines the impact of shape functions and mesh refinement levels on the accuracy of finite element solutions for the Stokes equations. We analyze the convergence of the velocity and pressure fields using a straightforward, uniform mesh discretization. The findings demonstrate that the convergence rate for the velocity is contingent upon the polynomial degree of the shape functions, whereas the pressure convergence rate is influenced by both the shape functions and the mesh refinement level.

The statefinder parameters, denoted as $\{r, s\}$, serve as a diagnostic tool to differentiate between various cosmological models, including $\Lambda$CDM. This study examines the behavior of these parameters within a braneworld framework featuring a scalar field, where the model's dynamics are governed by a specific potential. We derive the statefinder expressions for this scenario and analyze their evolution across various potential forms. Our findings indicate that the statefinder trajectories for this braneworld model deviate from those of $\Lambda$CDM, thereby offering a means to distinguish the two.

Tidal disruption events (TDEs) involving supermassive black holes (SMBHs) are hypothesized to generate relativistic jets capable of producing high-energy neutrinos and gamma rays. This study examines the impact of shock obliquity and velocity on the resulting particle energy spectra and neutrino fluxes. We find that the resulting spectra are highly sensitive to shock obliquity, with the most extreme cases yielding a power-law index of $\Gamma \approx 2.2$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the neutrino flux from TDEs is significantly influenced by the SMBH's spin and the resulting shock velocity.

This study investigates the acoustic cavitation behavior of bubbles formed within a polymer gel. We demonstrate that the material properties of these bubbles can be adjusted by varying the polymer concentration, thereby influencing the threshold for bubble inception and the resulting dynamics. Specifically, bubbles nucleated in gels with higher concentrations exhibit a significantly lower inception threshold compared to those in water. Furthermore, the oscillation dynamics of these bubbles are markedly distinct from those in water, characterized by a prolonged period of stable oscillation before transitioning into chaotic behavior.

This paper introduces a novel approach to detecting stress in continuous speech by integrating emotion recognition. We propose a new dataset featuring stress-labeled continuous speech paired with emotion annotations. Our methodology involves a two-stage process: first, classifying emotions in audio segments, and second, utilizing these classifications to enhance stress detection. Experimental results demonstrate that this two-stage framework outperforms current state-of-the-art methods for stress detection.

This paper introduces a speech annotation system that leverages the synergy between databases and cloud storage. The system's architecture is designed to enhance both the efficiency and effectiveness of the annotation workflow.

This study examines the chemical evolution of the Milky Way's disk, specifically focusing on the influence of the initial mass function (IMF) on the abundance of alpha elements. We employ a chemical evolution model that accounts for the Milky Way's disk's formation and evolution, incorporating a variable IMF. Our findings indicate that the Milky Way's disk is likely composed of two distinct stellar populations: an older, metal-poor component and a younger, metal-rich one. We demonstrate that the observed alpha-element abundances in the Milky Way's disk can be explained by a model featuring a top-heavy IMF in the early universe, which subsequently transitions to a standard IMF. Furthermore, we explore the implications of these results for the Milky Way's formation and evolution.

This paper introduces a group-based sparse representation technique designed to enhance the computational efficiency of dictionary learning. While conventional methods typically rely on greedy algorithms like Matching Pursuit (MP) or Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP), these approaches often struggle with high computational costs and limited scalability when dealing with large-scale data. Our proposed method addresses these limitations by leveraging the inherent group structure of the dictionary to significantly accelerate the learning process. Specifically, we develop a group-based greedy algorithm that utilizes a novel greedy criterion to select groups of atoms rather than individual atoms. This approach not only reduces the number of required iterations but also improves the overall speed of the algorithm. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this method achieves superior performance compared to traditional greedy algorithms. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

This paper introduces a novel lightweight block named REthinker, designed to enhance the performance of existing Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The block's primary objective is to improve the network's sensitivity to specific object classes by leveraging the attention mechanism. It achieves this by aggregating the most relevant features from the preceding layer and applying them to the current layer's feature maps. The proposed architecture is highly efficient, requiring only 1.5 times the parameters and 2.5 times the computational cost of a standard convolutional layer. We evaluated the block's effectiveness by integrating it into the ResNet-50 architecture, resulting in a 0.7% increase in top-1 accuracy on the ImageNet-1K dataset. Furthermore, the model demonstrated superior performance on the COCO dataset, achieving a 0.7% increase in mean average precision (mAP) and a 0.7% increase in average precision (AP). The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/DeepLearning4All/REthinker.
